content: Stellar evolution describes how stars form, change, and ultimately end their lives through processes governed by the balance between gravity and pressure. Stars begin as diffuse clouds of hydrogen and helium gas (nebulae). Gravitational collapse of these clouds increases density and temperature until the core reaches approximately 10 million Kelvin, initiating nuclear fusion where hydrogen nuclei combine to form helium, releasing enormous energy through mass conversion (E=mcÂ²). This energy creates outward pressure that counterbalances gravity, establishing hydrostatic equilibriumâthe defining characteristic of a main sequence star. A star's mass primarily determines its evolution: more massive stars burn hotter, appear bluer, and exhaust their fuel faster than less massive stars. Our Sun, a medium-mass star, will remain on the main sequence for about 10 billion years total. After depleting core hydrogen, stars expand into red giants as fusion continues in shells around an inert helium core, which eventually becomes hot enough to fuse into carbon and oxygen. Stellar endpoints differ dramatically by mass: low-mass stars (< 8 solar masses) shed outer layers as planetary nebulae, leaving behind dense white dwarfs that slowly cool over billions of years; intermediate-mass stars (8-40 solar masses) end in spectacular supernova explosions, leaving neutron stars with matter so compressed that electrons and protons combine; massive stars (> 40 solar masses) may also form black holes after supernovae, with gravity so intense that nothing, not even light, escapes. These stellar remnantsâwhite dwarfs, neutron stars, and black holesârepresent the final stages of stellar evolution, while the ejected material enriches the interstellar medium with heavier elements, providing building blocks for new generations of stars and planets.

scenario.title: Stellar Campfire Simulator
scenario.content: Students manage virtual campfires that model stellar processes, observing how different initial conditions produce various evolutionary paths. The simulation draws parallels between campfire stages and stellar phases: fuel gathering represents nebula formation, ignition represents fusion initiation, steady burning represents main sequence stability, and final stages represent various stellar endpoints. The system visualizes energy production, gravitational forces, and element creation throughout the stellar lifecycle. Students can manipulate initial mass, composition, and environmental factors to observe how these affect stellar evolution. Interactive tools allow students to accelerate time to observe complete stellar lifecycles, examine cross-sectional views of stellar interiors, and track the production and distribution of elements. Challenge scenarios task students with creating specific types of stellar remnants or optimizing conditions for the development of habitable planetary systems, teaching astrophysical principles through an accessible and engaging analog.

hypothesis.description: Students will model stellar lifecycles by analyzing the relationship between mass, energy production, and evolutionary endpoints. They will predict how stars of different masses evolve through various stages, and explain the physical processes that drive stellar transformation from birth to final remnants.
